text.p: Copper prices rebounded on the LME on Wednesday, giving a boost to other metals.
Oil was hit by late profit-taking in New York but wheat rose on concerns about flooding in some U.S. grain regions.
Gold also firmed, helping the push up the CRB index by 0.41 points to 244.75.

LME copper rebounded from a test near the psychological $2,300 per tonne level on Wednesday afternoon, giving a late boost to several other metals. Successive waves of selling, largely fund liquidation, pressured three month copper prices, which bottomed out at $2,305 before prices bounced on short-covering and trade buying. The market finished with pared losses of $8 at $2,325, but remained mired below the 30-day moving average of $2,331. "It's still a bearish close and suggests that we'll come down to fill a gap that extends to $2,295," said analyst Robin Bahr of broker Brandeis.

Nickel joined copper in a modest rally, bouncing off a low of $7,870 to finish the day back above the 30-day moving average and within striking distance of the $8,000 mark. The market ended with a gain of $80 at $7,985, but needs to move convincingly back above $8,000 before the bearish tone can be dispelled, Bahr said. "Until we regain the $8,000 level, any rallies will be sold into," he said.

Aluminium also got a minor boost from copper's rebound, prying itself loose of the $1,640 level it had held most of the day to close at its high of $1,647, a gain of $5. The market was still ensconced between the 10-day and 30-day moving averages, the latter which should offer support at $1,634.

Zinc woke up on the afternoon kerb and marched towards the $1,300 level, topping out $2 shy of the psychological target after earlier in the day extending as low as $1,282. Last business on the kerb was near the highs at $1,296, up $6. The market seemed to be consolidating before re-attacking Monday's fresh peak of $1,307, chartists said.

The rallies in the others, however, failed to stimulate lead, pressured by Far Eastern selling after stalling at peaks of $710 for the past two days. But the market clawed off its low of $686 to end $17 weaker at $691. The move above $700 had been largely option-inspired ahead of Third Wednesday pricing, but now the March date has passed, prices could slide further, Bahr said. "There may not be anything to hold it up now," he said.

COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended higher Wednesday on good volume, with traders increasingly of the belief the complex may have found a bottom after gold slid back below $350 this week. "I like the technical aspects in gold and there looks to be strong physical demand in below $350 an ounce," PaineWebber commodities research director, Bernard Savaiko, said. COMEX April gold found support at $346.30 Tuesday and gained a further $2.50 Wednesday to close at $353.00 an ounce, after seeing a session high at $354.50. Gold was fixed in London at $349.10.

NYMEX crude abruptly turned negative late session and ended lower Wednesday on profit-taking after a rally in oil prices pushed crude up almost $1.75 a barrel in two days. "We had some late session profit-taking by longs, so they could get out of the way before tomorrow's expiry. We had gone up in a hurry," said a New York crude trader. April crude ended two cents a barrel lower at $22.04 after rising as much as 59 cents to $22.65. Mid-session, bullish oil inventory data and barge shipment delays pushed spot crude through resistance levels, triggering buy stops, dealers said.

CBOT wheat futures closed higher on concerns about forecasts for spring flooding in the U.S. Midwest with a late rally in soybeans and soymeal also cited, traders said. "The flooding worries are a very real concern. But the sooner it floods and gets it out of the way the sooner they can plant (spring wheat)," a trader said. CBOT March wheat expired Wednesday at 1201 CST. The March went off the board one cent higher at $3.78. Wheat closed 7-3/4 cents per bushel higher to one cent lower, with May up 7-1/4 at $3.91.

New York world sugar futures settled weaker and near the day's lows but the May contract managed to hold support at 10.68 cents and maintain its recent trading range. The spot month closed down 0.13 cent at 10.75 cents per lb, having ranged from 10.88 cents to 10.71 cents.
